title: Grade 8 Computer Science: Data, Networks & Safety Online

learn: Computers use binary (base 2) because circuits are either on (1) or off (0).
Place values double: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
check: Computers use binary because circuits are...
lessons.try: Convert your age and birth day to binary.

learn: To convert decimal to binary, subtract the largest power of 2 repeatedly.
Check by converting back.
lessons.try: Convert 42 and 100 to binary.

learn: 8 bits = 1 byte; a byte holds 256 values (0-255).
Kilobyte (about 1,000 bytes), megabyte (about a million), gigabyte (about a billion), terabyte (about a trillion).
Hexadecimal (base 16) is a shorthand for binary, using 0-9 and A-F.
check: A byte holds values from 0 to...
lessons.try: Find the storage size of three files on a device.

learn: ASCII assigns numbers to characters: "A" = 65, "a" = 97.
Unicode extends this to over 140,000 characters in every language plus emoji.
UTF-8 is the most common Unicode encoding on the web.
check: The most common web encoding is...
lessons.try: Write a secret message using ASCII codes.

learn: Images are grids of pixels; each pixel stores red, green and blue values (0-255 each).
Resolution is the number of pixels; colour depth is bits per pixel.
Compression (like JPEG) shrinks files by removing some detail.
lessons.try: Use a pixel editor to make an 8 × 8 image.

learn: Sound waves are sampled thousands of times a second.
CD audio uses 44,100 samples per second.
Higher sample rates and bit depth give better quality but larger files.
check: CD audio uses ___ samples per second.
lessons.try: Record yourself at two quality settings and compare file sizes.

learn: Data is information collected for analysis: numbers, text, images.
Quantitative data is numerical; qualitative data is descriptive.
Data can be collected by surveys, sensors, observations and websites.
lessons.try: List data your phone collects.

learn: Spreadsheets organise data in rows (records) and columns (fields).
Formulas calculate: =SUM(A1:A10), =AVERAGE(B2:B20).
Sorting and filtering find patterns.
check: In a spreadsheet, a column is a...
lessons.try: Make a spreadsheet of your weekly screen time.

learn: Good data is accurate, complete and consistent.
Cleaning data fixes errors, duplicates and missing values.
Biased collection leads to misleading results.
lessons.try: Clean a messy sample data set.

learn: Analysis looks for trends, averages, outliers and relationships.
Correlation means two variables change together; it doesn't prove one causes the other.
Ice cream sales and sunburns correlate because both rise in summer.
check: Correlation proves causation. True or false?
Ice cream and sunburns both rise because of...
lessons.try: Find a correlation in a data set and explain whether it's causation.

learn: Bar charts compare categories; line graphs show change over time; pie charts show parts of a whole.
Scatter plots show relationships between two variables.
Label axes and include a title.
check: Change over time is best shown by a...
Parts of a whole is shown by a...
lessons.try: Make three different charts from one data set.

learn: Truncated axes can exaggerate differences.
Cherry-picked data hides the full picture.
Always check scales, sources and sample sizes.
check: Starting an axis above zero can...
lessons.try: Find a misleading graph online and explain the trick.

learn: The internet is a global network of networks connecting billions of devices.
Data travels in small pieces called packets that may take different routes.
Packets are reassembled at their destination.
check: The internet is a network of...
lessons.try: Act out sending packets as a class, using paper notes.

learn: Every device has an IP address.
DNS translates names like example.com into IP addresses, like a phone book.
Protocols are rules: TCP/IP for delivery, HTTP for web pages, HTTPS for secure web pages.
check: HTTPS is the ___ version of HTTP.
lessons.try: Look at a website's address bar and find the padlock for HTTPS.

learn: The internet is the infrastructure; the World Wide Web is a service that runs on it.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the web in 1989.
Email, video calls and games also use the internet.
lessons.try: List five internet services that aren't the web.

learn: The CPU executes instructions; RAM holds working data; storage keeps data long-term.
The motherboard connects components; the GPU handles graphics.
Input, output and storage devices connect to the system.
lessons.try: Label a diagram of computer components.

learn: A LAN (local area network) connects devices in a home or school.
A WAN (wide area network) spans large areas; the internet is the largest WAN.
Routers direct traffic; Wi-Fi connects wirelessly.
lessons.try: Draw a diagram of your home network.

learn: Bandwidth is how much data can travel per second, measured in bits per second.
Latency is the delay before data arrives.
Fibre-optic cables carry data as light, very fast.
lessons.try: Run a speed test with a parent's permission and interpret the results.

learn: Malware includes viruses, worms, ransomware and spyware.
Phishing uses fake messages to steal information.
Social engineering tricks people rather than computers.
lessons.try: Identify phishing signs in sample emails.

learn: Use strong, unique passwords and a password manager.
Turn on two-factor authentication.
Keep software updated to fix security holes.
lessons.try: Check a device's update and security settings with a parent.

learn: Accessing systems without permission is illegal.
Ethical hackers test security with permission to make systems safer.
Report security problems responsibly.
lessons.try: Discuss why permission matters in cybersecurity.

learn: Encryption scrambles data so only authorised people can read it.
The Caesar cipher shifts letters: with shift 3, A becomes D.
Modern encryption uses complex maths and keys.
check: With a Caesar shift of 3, A becomes...
lessons.try: Encode and decode a message with a Caesar cipher.

learn: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key.
Public-key encryption uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock.
HTTPS uses this to protect web traffic.
check: The private key is used to...
lessons.try: Explain public-key encryption with a padlock analogy.

learn: Websites and apps collect data about you: location, searches, contacts.
Privacy settings let you control what you share.
Think before sharing personal information.
lessons.try: Review the privacy settings of an app with a parent.

learn: Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave online.
Posts, photos and comments can last forever.
Colleges and employers may look at it.
check: Who might look at your footprint?
lessons.try: Search your name (with a parent) and review what appears.

learn: Check the source, author, date and evidence.
Use lateral reading: open other tabs to see what others say about the source.
Be cautious of content designed to provoke strong emotions.
check: Content that provokes strong emotions should make you...
lessons.try: Fact-check a viral claim.

learn: Cyberbullying is using technology to harass others.
Upstanders report bullying and support targets.
Balance screen time with offline life.
lessons.try: Write a personal technology-use plan.

learn: Programs store data in lists: scores = [85, 92, 78].
Loop through data to calculate totals and averages.
Python: sum(scores) / len(scores) gives the mean.
lessons.try: Write a program that finds the average of a list of temperatures.

learn: Filter data with conditions: keep scores above 80.
Search for an item with a loop or "in".
Count matches with a counter variable.
lessons.try: Write a program that counts how many days were above 25 degrees.

learn: Choose a question, collect or find data, clean it, analyse it and present results.
Use code to calculate and charts to communicate.
Explain what the data does and doesn't show.
check: A data project starts with a...
lessons.try: Complete a mini data project on a topic you choose.
